card_headline: Touadéra starts a third term with the UN force renewed to 2027, Russia's role unsettled, fuel protests in Bangui and fighting on two borders.
card_summary: President Faustin-Archange Touadéra was sworn in for a third seven-year term on 30 March after an election the main opposition coalition boycotted. [2][1] The UN calls most of the country relatively stable, but armed groups are active in the south-east and on the Sudanese border. [3] About 2 million people face acute food insecurity, and the 2026 aid plan was 20.6 percent funded in June. [3] Petrol above 1,100 CFA francs a litre has brought protests and arrests. [8][20]
card_local: Local sourcing is thin in this draft. Tchadinfos, a regional outlet, reports that public television chiefs were briefly detained in January over an interrupted victory speech, citing the Bangui press network RJDH. [15]
card_international: AFP reports the detention of five civil society leaders who called a shutdown in Bangui, and Reuters reports the ICC conviction of a former Séléka figure. [20][10]
card_scholar: Crisis Group, as summarised by RFI, says the war in Sudan is a windfall for armed groups in Vakaga, and GI-TOC alleges a politically connected fuel cartel. [18][14]
context_md: The Séléka coalition ousted President François Bozizé in 2013, and the anti-balaka militia he armed in response fuelled further bloodshed until French troops and a UN mandate stabilised the country in 2014. [10] The country has been relatively stable since a 2019 peace agreement, Reuters writes. [10] Russia's Wagner Group deployed in 2018 at Touadéra's request and is credited with driving armed groups out of major cities, though violence persists in the east and north-west. [11] Touadéra has been in power since 2016, and a 2023 constitutional change removed presidential term limits. [22] GI-TOC notes that the UPC and 3R armed groups accepted peace deals in April 2025. [14] The UN peacekeeping mission, MINUSCA, was established in 2014. [5]

sections.title: A third term after a boycott, and arrests for critics
sections.body_md:
President Faustin-Archange Touadéra won a third term in the 28 December 2025 vote. Provisional results gave him 76.15 percent, against 14.66 percent for Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and 3.19 percent for Henri-Marie Dondra, on turnout of 52.42 percent. [1] RFI later reported his final share as 77.90 percent. [2] The main opposition coalition, the BRDC, boycotted the vote, and Dologuélé and Dondra both alleged fraud, which the government denies. [1] A 2023 constitutional change removed term limits and, according to Human Rights Watch, lengthened presidential terms from five to seven years. [22] Touadéra was sworn in on 30 March 2026. [2] On 15 May he reappointed Félix Moloua as prime minister, less than 48 hours after the government resigned. [16]

The state has answered criticism with detentions. On 20 January security forces briefly held the director general and programme director of public television after the broadcast of Touadéra's victory speech was cut for the evening news, according to Tchadinfos, which cites the RJDH. [15] In October five civil society leaders who had called a citywide shutdown on 12 October were arrested, and on 30 October they were placed in pretrial detention at the Camp de Roux prison. [20][23] Interior Minister Bienvenu Zokoué described the shutdown as an attempt to destabilise institutions and said the leaders had ties to two opposition parties. [20] The BRDC denies working with rebels. [23] On 21 October Touadéra declined to intervene, saying the matter belongs to the courts, and the detainees' lawyer says they began a hunger strike. [21]

On 13 November hundreds of people marched in Bangui against the cost of living, with the authorities' permission. [8] Petrol sells above 1,100 CFA francs a litre and the BRDC is asking for 850. [8] Africanews reports no government response to the march. [8]

lenses.local: Tchadinfos, a regional outlet, reports the public television arrests and cites the Bangui press network RJDH. [15]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, AFP and Africanews carry the election result, the arrests and the march. [1][20][8]
lenses.scholar: Human Rights Watch's World Report 2026 notes that UN experts urged reform of the electoral authority in June 2025 over its internal dysfunction. [22]

sections.title: A calmer centre, an active south-east and a Sudan border that is heating up
sections.body_md:
The Secretary-General's June report calls the situation relatively stable in most of the country, with fragile areas in the north-west, the east and the south-east. [3] It counts 222 security incidents involving UN personnel between February and 1 June, including three peacekeeper deaths, and 103 transhumance incidents that caused at least 41 deaths. [3] On 1 June 427,479 people were internally displaced, and 732,977 Central Africans were refugees abroad. [3]

The south-east is the active front. The Zande militia AAKG formed in March 2023, Wagner trained about 200 of its fighters, and the government suspended their integration into the army in May 2025, after which the militia fragmented, Crisis Group reports. [12] Fighting around Zémio in early January between the army and its allies and the AAKG left nearly 2,000 displaced people sheltering at the town's hospital and church, the ICRC said. [24] In July OCHA suspended activities in Haut-Mbomou, which hosts about 6,000 refugees and about 20,000 displaced people, RFI reported. [19]

The north-east is the newer front. An armed group attacked Am-Dafock, in Vakaga on the Sudanese border, on 30 June. The toll is disputed: Xinhua, a state outlet, reported 3 dead and 18 injured, while RFI puts the dead at about thirty. [17][18] Valentine Rugwabiza, the UN's top official in the country, told the Security Council that civilians and security personnel died, six peacekeepers were wounded and 17,000 people were displaced. [4] The prime minister visited Birao and told armed groups to join the disarmament programme. [25] Crisis Group's report of 29 October, as summarised by RFI, says refugees, fighters and arms crossing from Sudan are helping Central African armed groups rebuild, and that Birao's population has doubled in three years. [18] Rugwabiza reported 1,907 fighters disarmed since July 2025. [4]

lenses.local: Local sourcing is thin here. RFI's dispatches from Haut-Mbomou and Vakaga are the closest to ground reporting in this draft. [19][18]
lenses.international: Africanews and Xinhua carry the Am-Dafock attack, with different casualty figures. [25][17]
lenses.scholar: Crisis Group finds the AAKG fragmented, with weak and disputed leadership that makes negotiation harder. [12]

sections.title: Russia: the Wagner to Africa Corps handover is unfinished and contested
sections.body_md:
Russia arrived in late 2017 with about 175 instructors after obtaining a UN arms embargo exemption, the Congressional Research Service writes. It gives about 2,100 as the 2021 peak and about 1,500 for early 2026, and describes both as reported figures. [6] Touadéra campaigned on his security record after enlisting Russian contractors and Rwandan soldiers. [1] Human Rights Watch says security in major towns still relies on Wagner. [22]

Who is in charge of the Russian presence is the open question. The CRS says the Africa Corps appears to have taken control of former Wagner networks, and that Touadéra resisted Moscow's pressure to pay for defence services directly. [6] An AFP report from early 2026 quoted an unnamed European military source saying Moscow had failed to convince Touadéra to switch, while Touadéra said talks were under way and denied pressure. [11] He visited Russia from 1 to 5 March. [3] DW reported on 30 March that the Africa Corps was set to take over in Bangui, and that Bangui media had reported Wagner wanted 900 billion CFA francs, about US$1.6 billion, to leave. [26] The presidential spokesperson, Albert Yaloké Mokpem, called that claim an attempt to create panic, and DW says it is unconfirmed and calls the sum unrealistic. [26]

Sergey Eledinov, founder of Convoy Africa, argued in African Arguments in August that the transition is incomplete and that Russia's security, mining and information activities now form a system Moscow cannot easily leave. That is one author's view. [27] HRW records that former 3R members said in August 2025 that Wagner fighters attacked their bases, killing one person and injuring three. This is their account. [22]

lenses.local: Bangui media first carried the 900 billion CFA francs claim, and the presidency denies it. [26]
lenses.international: AFP, DW and the Congressional Research Service describe a handover that has not been confirmed by either government. [11][26][6]
lenses.scholar: African Arguments carries an analysis that the Russian presence has become self-sustaining. [27]

sections.title: Fuel, gold and diamonds: where the money goes
sections.body_md:
Fuel is where the cost of living meets politics. In July the official pump price in Bangui was 1,100 CFA francs a litre, and roadside resellers charged 1,500 during a shortage that had lasted about ten days. [28] The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) reported in November 2025 that diesel cost US$2.17 a litre in mid-2025 in a country where 70 percent of people live on less than US$1.90 a day. [14] It estimates US$17.5 to 30 million in excess revenue in 2024 and says Neptune Oil, a Cameroonian firm, handled about 70 percent of imports. [14] An independent audit by the firm CPCS, requested by the IMF and dated October 2025, found that an unexplained price gap costs the state nearly 1 billion CFA francs a month, and that transport fees ran at 15 percent against a 10 percent contract ceiling. [29] The BRDC wants the state's agreement with Neptune Oil published. [23]

GI-TOC says activity linked to Wagner at the Ndassima gold mine generates an estimated US$100 million a year, with no declared output and no recorded exports. [30] The same authors report that a 177-carat rough diamond disappeared in January 2025 weeks after the export ban was lifted, and that a reported US$5 million sale was cancelled after Wagner's leader in the country intervened. [30] The Rio Times reports that the Kimberley Process lifted remaining restrictions in November 2024, and that the state cannot yet verify who holds which mining right while a cadastre is built with World Bank support. [13]

The IMF projects 2.6 percent growth and 1.5 percent inflation for 2026. [9] The World Bank projected 2.7 percent growth for 2025, after 1.5 percent in 2024, and listed fuel shortages and fragile security as risks. [31] The Rio Times gives 4.5 percent for 2025, which conflicts with the World Bank release and is not used here. [13] The World Bank's July review says domestic revenue is below 10 percent of GDP and the wage bill absorbs up to 73 percent of public resources. [32]

lenses.local: RFI quotes Bangui motorcyclists and residents on queues and reseller prices, and says the Energy Ministry had not responded. [28]
lenses.international: AFP and Africanews report the fuel price protests and the arrests that followed. [20][8]
lenses.scholar: GI-TOC describes a cartel-like fuel sector, while the World Bank frames the fiscal problem as low revenue and a large wage bill. [14][32]

sections.title: Two million people short of food and an aid plan about a fifth funded
sections.body_md:
The 2026 humanitarian response plan says 2.3 million people, 35 percent of the population, rely on aid. It targets 1.3 million people and asks for US$264.1 million. [33] The Secretary-General's June report says about 2 million people, 31 percent of the population, face IPC phase 3 or worse, including about 262,000 in phase 4. [3] The plan was 20.6 percent funded on 1 June, and aid had reached 306,900 of the 1.3 million targeted by the end of April. [3] Rugwabiza told the Security Council in October that the plan was less than half funded. [4]

Sudan's war adds refugees to a thin system. The country hosted 35,048 Sudanese refugees in March 2026, many in Birao, and Africanews reports that more than 120 humanitarian bases run by 60 organisations have closed since 2025 for lack of funds, six of them in Vakaga. [34] The Secretary-General reports 60,649 refugees and asylum seekers in total, 36,114 of them Sudanese, and 44 humanitarian access incidents between February and June. [3] The IPC snapshot for April to August 2025 put 2.2 million people in phase 3 or above, with 481,000 in phase 4. [35]

lenses.international: Africanews describes the refugee situation as severe and largely overlooked. [34]
lenses.scholar: The IPC analysis names conflict, poor harvests and economic shocks as drivers, and says violence limits access to farmland in the south-east, north-east and north-west. [35]

sections.title: MINUSCA stays until November 2027 as its money runs short
sections.body_md:
The Security Council extended MINUSCA to 15 November 2027 by a unanimous vote. France drafted the text, which adjusts troop levels and backs a pilot garrison army project. [5] The mission fields more than 12,000 peacekeepers, and Rugwabiza warned the Council against a premature exit. [4] Liberia, speaking also for the DRC and Somalia, said "A task handed over must remain a task delivered." [5] Unpaid assessed contributions to the mission's account were US$452.6 million on 1 June, and liquidity limits cut spending by 15 percent and sent 4,031 military personnel home. [3] A separate resolution, 2827, extended the sanctions regime on armed groups to 31 July 2027 and its panel of experts to 31 August 2027. [36]

Courts are moving on past crimes. The ICC convicted the former Séléka figure Mahamat Said Abdel Kani of crimes against humanity, including torture, on 23 September, and acquitted him on three war crimes counts. Sentencing comes later. [10] HRW records that in 2025 the Special Criminal Court convicted FPRC members of war crimes and crimes against humanity, several in absentia. [22] The Secretary-General's report attributes 423 violations against 883 victims in its period to state actors, 68 percent of them deprivation of liberty or detention conditions, and 254 abuses against 314 victims to armed groups. [3]

lenses.international: Africanews and Reuters (via Al Jazeera) carry the mandate renewal and the ICC verdict. [5][10]
lenses.scholar: Human Rights Watch and the Secretary-General's report supply the main accountability record. [22][3]

sections.title: Press freedom: criminal penalties are back and RSF's rank has fallen to 81
sections.body_md:
Reporters Without Borders ranks the country 81st of 180 in its 2026 index, down from 72nd, with a score of 56.73 against 60.15. [7] Radio dominates, there are only two television channels, and print is mostly limited to Bangui. [7] RSF also says a foreign agents law modelled on Russian legislation has been under study since October 2024. [7] The National Assembly restored criminal penalties for press offences in May 2025, reversing a 2020 decriminalisation. [22] RSF says the publishing director Ulrich Landry Nguéma Ngokpélé was arrested on 8 May 2025 and detained six days later, and HRW says his charges were later changed to violating the press law. [7][22]

Influence operations are a second story. Forbidden Stories reported in November 2024 that a former propagandist, Ephrem Yalike, said a Russian handler recruited him in 2019, paid him per article and had sponsored pieces placed in Bangui newspapers. [37] RSF says Russian actors have reportedly built media outlets and networks since 2018. [7] Radio Ndeke Luka, the most listened-to station, broadcasts in French and Sango from Bangui through 13 FM transmitters, according to its founder, Fondation Hirondelle, and RSF says it reportedly faces regular pressure. [38][7]

lenses.local: Radio Ndeke Luka is the main Bangui voice in French and Sango, but this draft did not read its own reporting. [38]
lenses.international: RSF and HRW are the main international sources on the press law and the arrests. [7][22]
lenses.scholar: Forbidden Stories' investigation documents paid placements, based chiefly on one named source. [37]

factchecks.claim: Russian security support has brought peace to the Central African Republic.
factchecks.by: Simplice Sarandji, president of the National Assembly, speaking to Sputnik Africa (March 2024)
factchecks.evidence: VOA's Polygraph called the claim misleading. It cited a US State Department report accusing Wagner forces of razing villages and killing civilians, and a joint investigation finding Wagner gains access to raw materials in exchange for military support. It also cited the Crisis Group's February 2024 view that security remained precarious. The UN's June 2026 report calls most of the country relatively stable but names fragile areas in the north-west, east and south-east.

factchecks.evidence: The fact-check republished by AllAfrica cites AP reporting from April 2024 that Russian forces became one of the most violent armed groups in the country. It cites RFE/RL reporting, using ACLED data, of more than 100 fights and 362 incidents of violence against civilians by Russian troops from 2018 to 2024, with at least 786 deaths. The page does not name the original fact-checker, and these figures were not independently checked here.

gaps: Local sourcing is thin: no article from a Bangui-based outlet was read directly. Radio Ndeke Luka, Oubangui Médias and Corbeau News Centrafrique could not be fetched or confirmed for dated stories, and the one local-type source is a regional outlet in Chad.
The Am-Dafock toll is contested (3 dead per Xinhua, about thirty per RFI, no official figure); no UN or government count was found.
The final presidential result (77.90 percent) and the Constitutional Court ruling rest on RFI's summary; the court's decision was not read.
Crisis Group's 29 October report on Sudan and Vakaga was read only through RFI's summary; the CPCS fuel audit was read only through RFI.
Russian troop numbers are reported estimates in a CRS brief, not confirmed counts, and no Russian or Central African government source was read on the Africa Corps handover.
Neptune Oil's and the government's responses to the GI-TOC and audit findings were not found; GI-TOC figures are its own estimates.
The Security Council sanctions press release (SC/16424) shows no date; July 2026 is inferred.
ACLED, UCDP and Freedom House data were not accessed, so conflict fatality counts and a democracy score are missing.
Reporter entries are limited to bylines and profiles seen this session; the podcast episode lacks host, guest, date and length on its page.
Books: only titles with a bookseller, press or review page seen this session are listed; Hunting Game was not read.

name: Central African Republic

scores.coverage_basis: AFP, Reuters and Xinhua file on the country mainly when something breaks, such as the election, the Am-Dafock attack, the fuel protest arrests and the ICC verdict. [1][20][10][17] RFI and Africanews follow it more regularly, and Africanews describes the refugee crisis as largely overlooked. [19][34] Local sourcing is thin, and RSF says the press is small and under pressure. [7]

severity.basis: The UN calls most of the country relatively stable, but records 222 incidents involving UN personnel in four months, at least 41 deaths in transhumance incidents, and attacks in Haut-Mbomou and Vakaga. [3][4]
About 2 million people face acute food insecurity, 427,479 are displaced, and the 2026 aid plan was 20.6 percent funded on 1 June. [3]
The main opposition boycotted the election, five civil society leaders were detained, criminal penalties for press offences were restored, and RSF's rank fell from 72 to 81. [1][21][22][7]
GI-TOC says 70 percent of people live on less than US$1.90 a day, and the World Bank says revenue is below 10 percent of GDP with the wage bill taking up to 73 percent of public resources. [14][32]
The UN reports fewer violations and falling displacement, but a new Sudan border front, fuel protests and detentions of activists cut the other way. [3][18][21]

parts.basis: Russia has an estimated 1,500 personnel and mining interests, France drafted the MINUSCA renewal, and RFI reports growing UAE influence on the Sudan border. [6][5][18]
Gold and diamond output is largely artisanal, with exports mostly undeclared, and the economy is small. [30][13]
Fighters, arms and refugees move across the Sudanese border, and thousands of people from Haut-Mbomou crossed into the DRC. [18][39]
732,977 Central Africans are refugees abroad, and the country hosts 60,649 refugees and asylum seekers. [3]
The Russian private-security model, a UN mission now in its second decade and a hybrid national court alongside ICC trials all test international practice. [27][5][22][10]

summary: The Central African Republic matters beyond its borders mainly through Russia's presence, the Sudan war's spillover into Vakaga and the UN peacekeeping model, rather than through trade. [6][18][5] Its mineral exports are small and mostly undeclared, which keeps the economic score low. [30]
gi.up: A confirmed Africa Corps takeover with a new base, or a collapse of the Sudan border front pulling in the RSF.
gi.down: A durable disarmament of the FPRC and AAKG and a verified, orderly handover of MINUSCA tasks.

local_md:
Tchadinfos, a regional outlet, reports the public television arrests and cites the Bangui press network RJDH. [15]

Local sourcing is thin here. RFI's dispatches from Haut-Mbomou and Vakaga are the closest to ground reporting in this draft. [19][18]

Bangui media first carried the 900 billion CFA francs claim, and the presidency denies it. [26]

RFI quotes Bangui motorcyclists and residents on queues and reseller prices, and says the Energy Ministry had not responded. [28]

Radio Ndeke Luka is the main Bangui voice in French and Sango, but this draft did not read its own reporting. [38]
international_md:
Al Jazeera, AFP and Africanews carry the election result, the arrests and the march. [1][20][8]

Africanews and Xinhua carry the Am-Dafock attack, with different casualty figures. [25][17]

AFP, DW and the Congressional Research Service describe a handover that has not been confirmed by either government. [11][26][6]

AFP and Africanews report the fuel price protests and the arrests that followed. [20][8]

Africanews describes the refugee situation as severe and largely overlooked. [34]

Africanews and Reuters (via Al Jazeera) carry the mandate renewal and the ICC verdict. [5][10]

RSF and HRW are the main international sources on the press law and the arrests. [7][22]
scholar_md:
Human Rights Watch's World Report 2026 notes that UN experts urged reform of the electoral authority in June 2025 over its internal dysfunction. [22]

Crisis Group finds the AAKG fragmented, with weak and disputed leadership that makes negotiation harder. [12]

African Arguments carries an analysis that the Russian presence has become self-sustaining. [27]

GI-TOC describes a cartel-like fuel sector, while the World Bank frames the fiscal problem as low revenue and a large wage bill. [14][32]

The IPC analysis names conflict, poor harvests and economic shocks as drivers, and says violence limits access to farmland in the south-east, north-east and north-west. [35]

Human Rights Watch and the Secretary-General's report supply the main accountability record. [22][3]

Forbidden Stories' investigation documents paid placements, based chiefly on one named source. [37]
